facts.text: Birkenhead, across the River Mersey from Liverpool, grew from about 200 people in 1821 to more than 24,000 in 1851.
In 1840 a British parliamentary committee on the health of towns said action was needed to protect the poor from conditions caused by fast-growing urban populations.
An 1843 Act of Parliament let the Birkenhead Improvement Commissioners borrow money to buy land for a public park.
Joseph Paxton, head gardener at Chatsworth, designed Birkenhead Park in the 1840s.
Plots around the edge of Birkenhead Park were set aside for villas, and selling them was meant to recover the cost of the park.
Birkenhead Park officially opened on 5 April 1847 before a crowd of about 10,000 people.

Other city parks of the time had mostly been donated by wealthy people or needed subscriptions or entry fees; Birkenhead Park was bought and built with public money and was free for all visitors whatever their social class.
Birkenhead Park was the first park in Britain paid for with public money; Wirral Council calls it the first publicly funded park in the world.
Birkenhead Park covers 125 acres (50 hectares).
Frederick Law Olmsted (1822 to 1903) made his first trip to England in 1850.
On a trip to England, Olmsted was inspired by Birkenhead Park, which he described to his father as a people's garden.
Olmsted wrote that the poorest British farm worker was as free to enjoy every part of Birkenhead Park as the British queen.
Olmsted described his English journey in Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England, published in 1852.
Before Central Park, the only places many New Yorkers could find fresh air and open grass were cemeteries.
The New York State Legislature approved the creation of Central Park in 1853.
The Central Park site was rocky and swampy, and the city got it only because it was unsuitable for real estate development.
The Central Park Commission, set up in 1857, held a design competition for the fast-growing city and considered 33 entries.
The winning entry was the Greensward Plan by Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux, and Olmsted co-designed Central Park in 1858.
The Greensward Plan sank the roads that cross the park below ground level, so vehicles and people on foot could pass through at the same time.
On the second Sunday Central Park was open, in December 1858, about 10,000 New Yorkers visited, many of them to ice-skate.
Central Park covers about 843 acres.
Central Park (about 843 acres) is more than 6 times the size of Birkenhead Park (125 acres).
Birkenhead Park was a major influence on Olmsted's design of Central Park in New York.

notes: 選文數字對照：200（1821）、24,000（1851）、1843、1847、10,000（開幕人數）、1850、1852、1853、1858、33、10,000（1858 年 12 月第二個星期日的人數）、843 英畝。注意：Wirral Council 自稱「世界第一座公費公園」，但其他資料（Historic England、NEH）只寫「英國第一座」；選文只用「英國第一座」的說法。Olmsted 首次赴英是 1850 年（NPS），參觀 Birkenhead 是該次旅程（NPS John Olmsted 頁、NEH）。
